messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiet's eyes still welled up with tears whenever he thought about his granddaughter's near-fatal illness. It had been two years since the hospital ordeal, but the memory of her tiny body hooked up to machines and tubes felt more real than any ordinary day that followed. As a nanny, Kiet had always been fiercely devoted to his family; now, the trauma had left him questioning everything he thought he knew about himself. He couldn't shake off the feeling that he had permanently changed for the worse – that he was no longer the same person who used to care for his loved ones with such ease and confidence. Kiet's mind often wandered back to those harrowing days, replaying every conversation with doctors, every beeping of machines, every cry from his granddaughter. He tried hard not to think about it, but the memories lingered, refusing to fade into the background like ordinary recollections. When they did surface, Kiet found himself lost in a world that felt more present than past – as if he was still standing beside his granddaughter's hospital bed, watching helplessly as she struggled to breathe. His inability to make sense of those events, to tell a clear story even to himself, had taken a toll on Kiet's self-perception. He saw himself as unrecognisable, someone who had lost control and couldn't regain it. This distorted view seeped into his relationships; he began distrusting others, wondering if they were hiding something behind their sympathetic smiles and words of encouragement. People, in general, seemed less genuine to Kiet now – even those closest to him. As a result, Kiet started avoiding anything that might trigger more painful memories or feelings of vulnerability. He stopped attending family gatherings, citing exhaustion from his nanny job as an excuse. At work, he became increasingly withdrawn, struggling to connect with the children in his care. His usual warmth and playfulness had given way to distraction – he kept himself occupied all the time, whether it was tidying up toys or scrolling through his phone. Kiet's avoidance extended to medical care; he stopped going for regular check-ups, fearing that doctors might detect some underlying condition that would only add to his anxiety. This decision weighed heavily on him, but Kiet rationalised that seeking help would be a sign of weakness – a confirmation that he had indeed changed for the worse. When memories of his granddaughter's illness resurfaced, as they often did, Kiet tried to suppress them, redirecting his thoughts towards more mundane concerns. Yet, these attempts at mental distraction only seemed to reinforce the loop of negative appraisals and traumatic memories. The more Kiet pushed away his emotions, the more convinced he became that people were not what they seemed – that even his own family might be hiding something from him. His memories, in turn, grew more vivid, as if feeding off his anxiety. It was this vicious cycle that finally brought Kiet to seek help – a reluctant admission that he needed guidance to navigate the darkness that had consumed him. For Kiet, therapy represented a daunting prospect – an invitation to confront the very fears and doubts he had tried so hard to suppress. But with each passing day, his need for answers grew stronger than his avoidance. He hoped that by facing his demons head-on, he might rediscover the person he once was – or, at the very least, learn to live with the person he had become.
